claims.text: The initial material is a homogeneous, as-cast, single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Under high mechanical loading in demanding service, the alloy loses toughness.
Stress-induced nanoscale brittle precipitates form under the proposed service conditions.
Grain-boundary segregation develops under the proposed service conditions.
Localized brittle precipitates and grain-boundary segregation cause premature crack nucleation.
Thermal aging or service-temperature exposure drives compositional fluctuations.
High strain rates or low temperatures, when combined with thermal exposure and mechanical loading, favor the proposed microstructural evolution.
Mechanical loading activates dislocation motion and localized stress concentrations.
Dislocation activity and localized stresses, combined with thermal exposure, promote segregation and secondary-phase precipitation.
The precipitates and segregated regions act as crack-initiation sites.
Cracks initiated at these microstructural features propagate by brittle fracture and reduce overall toughness.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, combined thermal and mechanical exposure will reduce fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, combined exposure will cause an earlier onset of brittle fracture.
Crack initiation will be observed preferentially at precipitate-rich regions.
The proposed behavior applies to cryogenic or high-strain-rate engineering service.
A controlled comparison should test as-cast and pre-aged specimens under otherwise matched extreme-service loading conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if pre-aged and as-cast specimens show no statistically significant differences in precipitate or segregation evolution and no earlier toughness loss or brittle-fracture onset in the pre-aged specimens.

contradictions.description: The baseline is described as lacking exposure to aggressive loading, but the experiment necessarily subjects the as-cast comparison specimens to extreme-service loading. Thus the textual baseline and experimental control are not defined identically.

The hypothesis describes precipitates as stress-induced, whereas the intervention and experiment rely on pre-aging before loading. This makes it unclear whether the claimed precipitates are induced by stress, by aging, or by their interaction.
